strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: clearly identifies feature entanglement in overlapping regions as a key limitation of prior object-decomposed trajectory methods (Tora, DragAnything), and proposes an intuitive fix via phase-decomposed (pre/interaction/post) collaborative trajectories.

Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple axes: visual quality (FVD/PSNR/SSIM/VBench), trajectory accuracy, a substantial user study (45% preference vs 17.74% for best baseline), and downstream robotic policy success rates on RLBench and SIMPLER.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of causal embedding, mask- vs point-based object representation, collaborative vs separate trajectories, and injection mechanism (cross-attention vs conv-based), along with robustness analyses to mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation, and imperfect prompts.

Practical contributions beyond the core method: a new 21k video-trajectory annotated dataset from Bridge, a user-friendly Gradio annotation tool, and clear discussion of how the design simplifies user interaction (brush masks, partial trajectory specification).

Honest and detailed limitations section (3D generalization, automatic segmentation failure rates on multi-object scenes, novel robot morphology generalization) with supporting quantitative evidence (e.g., Grounded-SAM success rates), which strengthens the paper's credibility.

Demonstrates generalization to diverse in-the-wild/out-of-domain objects and long, multi-step autoregressive video generation, indicating the method is not narrowly overfit to Bridge-specific scenarios.
weaknesses: Downstream action-planning results (Table 4) are mixed rather than uniformly superior: RoboMaster underperforms Tora on several tasks (e.g., put knife 0.76 vs 0.82, open microwave 0.54 vs 0.61), which somewhat undercuts the claim of consistently 'more reliable interaction videos' translating into better policies.

The improvement margins on standard video-quality metrics (PSNR 21.55 vs 21.24, SSIM 0.803 vs 0.788 relative to Tora) are fairly small despite a large gap in user preference, raising questions about whether FVD/PSNR/SSIM adequately capture the qualitative gains being claimed, and inviting concern about cherry-picked qualitative examples in Fig. 5/6.

Practical annotation burden is non-trivial: the method still depends on accurate phase transition detection/annotation (F1, F2), and automatic tools (Grounded-SAM) achieve only 0.14–0.21 success on multi-object scenes, meaning substantial manual curation was needed for the training set and would likely be needed at deployment/scale.

Core novelty is somewhat incremental — reframing trajectory decomposition from an object axis to a temporal/phase axis, combined with fairly standard mask-based appearance/shape embeddings and a lightweight conv-based injector — rather than introducing fundamentally new modeling machinery.

Main quantitative comparisons and dataset curation rely solely on Bridge for training the primary model; RLBench/SIMPLER are used only for a small-scale post-training/adaptation stage (1,300 pairs), limiting the strength of claims about broad applicability across embodiments and environments.

Some methodological details remain underspecified for reproducibility, e.g., precise criteria/thresholds for automatic phase segmentation (motion threshold τ), and how failure cases in transition detection are handled during training versus filtered out.

strengths: Clear, well-motivated technical contribution: decomposing interaction into pre-interaction/interaction/post-interaction phases and associating each with the 'dominant' object's features is an intuitive and effective solution to the multi-object feature entanglement problem in prior trajectory-controlled video generation methods (Tora, DragAnything).

Comprehensive baseline comparison: all key baselines (Tora, MotionCtrl, DragAnything, IRASim) are retrained on the same curated dataset for fair comparison, and RoboMaster consistently outperforms them across FVD, PSNR, SSIM, trajectory error, and most VBench metrics.

Thorough ablation studies isolate the contribution of each design choice (causal embedding, mask vs. point representation, collaborative vs. separate trajectories, motion injector vs. cross-attention), and additional robustness analyses (mask sparsity, trajectory perturbation) support the practical claims about tolerance to imprecise user input.

Strong qualitative and generalization evidence: extensive in-the-wild results (diverse OOD objects, diverse manipulation skills, auto-regressive long video generation) suggest the method generalizes beyond the training distribution (Bridge V2).

Good attention to usability: the annotation scheme (brush mask + phase-segmented trajectory) is simpler for users than requiring complete dual trajectories, and a user study (with 47% preference vs ~20% for the next best) supports perceptual quality gains.
Detailed reproducibility information provided in supplementary (dataset curation pipeline, network architecture table, Gradio annotation tool description).
weaknesses: No downstream validation of the stated motivating use case (generating robotic decision-making/training data) -- e.g., no experiments showing that policies trained on RoboMaster-generated videos improve over policies trained with baseline-generated videos or real data alone. This is the primary claimed application in the introduction but is left unvalidated.

VBench metric improvements (Table 3) are often marginal (e.g., aesthetic/imaging quality differ by <1 point and RoboMaster sometimes underperforms Tora on Aesthetic Quality), raising questions about the practical significance of the gains beyond FVD/trajectory error.

Evaluation relies on a single dataset (Bridge V2) with a fairly small test set (214 samples) for the main quantitative comparisons; broader multi-embodiment or multi-dataset validation would strengthen claims of general applicability.

The dominant/submissive object formulation appears limited to two-entity interactions; it is unclear how the framework would scale to manipulations involving three or more interacting objects, which is not discussed or tested.
No failure case analysis or discussion of when/why the collaborative trajectory design might break down beyond the brief generic limitations paragraph.

Statistical significance/variance is not reported for any of the quantitative comparisons (single-run point estimates), making it hard to judge robustness of the reported gains, especially the small VBench deltas.

Method is built entirely on top of a large pretrained CogVideoX-5B backbone; compute cost, training/inference efficiency, and comparison of parameter overhead of the motion injector relative to baselines is not discussed, limiting insight into practical deployment cost.
